    <title>Dave Rupert</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/dave-rupert</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/J0uMBzayYttWSDTK</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Jun 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Dave Rupert, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://daverupert.com">daverupert.com</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/dave-rupert">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>I’m Dave Rupert, a web developer from Austin, TX. I went to college in a time before web design was even a discipline and majored in Japanese. After living in Japan for three years I came back to the states to pursue web development full-time. I started a company called Paravel with two of my best friends Trent Walton and Reagan Ray. We did that for fifteen years with pretty great success then took some funding and tried our hand at a startup for two years. Now I currently write web components at Microsoft and in my spare time I’m busy with family, writing, gaming, and building plastic mech models from the Gundam anime series.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>This is the third major incarnation of my blog. My first biog I actually consider to be the paper zine I wrote in high school with my friend Michael Rice. It was very low-budget and small-time but got me addicted to the thrill of self-publishing. </p>
<p>When I graduated college I started the web version of that zine and made a blog chronicling my entrance into corporate life and my time living in Japan. It was a great outlet for me creatively as well as a way to stay connected to folks back home. I hosted a few other friends blogs as well as a forum and it made for a nice little co-op community of bloggers. </p>
<p>That project eventually folded and the current version of my site was started a couple years later after I got deeper into professional web development. My content shifted from day-in-the-life random observations to more a tech focused tone. I only posted a few times a year but a switch flipped in me when I met Jeffrey Zeldman and Eric Meyer at SXSW one year and it motivated me to pour more energy into blogging regularly.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>Most of my ideas come from my work experience, tangents I’m chasing down, or seeing an intersection of two completely unrelated ideas. It’s pretty whimsical and I don’t try to pigeon hole myself into only talking about websites, although most of my posts are tech adjacent in some way since that’s a big part of my life. I care about the Web, so I write about the Web.</p>
<p>I have hundreds of draft posts that I organize in a <a href="https://daverupert.com/2021/09/my-notion-blogging-kanban/">blogging kanban</a> which I originally created in Notion but now do in <a href="https://daverupert.com/2025/05/notion-to-obsidian/">Obsidian</a>. With too many drafts in a folder I had a hard time figuring out the state of my ideas, so the kanban adds structure to help get my posts across the finish line: published on my blog. </p>
<p>I like to say “it’s overkill, but it’s my overkill” because I’m not a linear thinker (ADHD), and I’m always working on five ideas at once. It really does help me get a grasp on my writing. I even created a “Deadpool” status so I can let half-baked ideas die. It’s not a particularly efficient process but it works for me.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>I have a nice recliner I like to write in. I also have a cool backyard office that is a great space but feels more like work and I prefer the coziness of the chair. Digging in and writing often happens after the kids go to bed when the house is finally quiet and nothing is being asked of me. Then I can put hands on keyboard and get some thoughts out.</p>
<p>I don’t treat it as something precious, but I think your environment absolutely influences your creative output. Whether it’s noisiness, cleanliness, or being surrounded by your favorite tools; our spaces (as well as music or general mental wellbeing) enables creativity. You can eke out creativity anywhere, but the right setting removes a barrier for getting into that flow state.</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>My website is built with Jekyll on Netlify. Nothing beats a folder full of markdown files. I also have a folder full of assets that I sync to Netlify using <a href="https://blog.jim-nielsen.com/2024/deploying-with-netlify-shortcuts/">Apple Shorctuts</a>. I’ve tried blogging platforms with databases in the past but you’re always fighting against comment spam and hacks and constant updates. A static site generator really smoothes out the technical overhead to I can focus on the writing.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>If I were to do it all again, I would maybe try a pen name. Having my name associated to my blog has done well for my career, but what if it wasn’t? What if the line between me and writing was a bit more blurry. Dave Rupert is just some guy, but Snake Renegade… he’s a hero. </p>
<p>I don’t actually have the energy to maintain that ruse for decades, but it might be nice … in these uncertain times … to have an online persona detached from the name you put on your résumé.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>The domain name is $18.99 per year but beyond that It costs $0 to run my blog. I used to run ads on my site that made me about $100 per year, but I think they ad vendor restructured their payouts and I said goodbye. It was more about a self-imposed third party script constraint than the handfuls of cash I made. I’m not opposed to folks monetizing their blog but ideally it’s tasteful. I probably get more upset at people who disable ads on small blogs than those that run ads on small blogs.</p>
<p>In a perfect world the <a href="https://webmonetization.org">Web Monetization API</a> would exist and we could passively drop pennies in people’s pockets as we travel from one site to the next. There was a whole crypto grift associated with Web Monetization though, so if they ever do it again I hope it can be more straightforward.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>One of my favorite bloggers is <a href="https://www.susanjeanrobertson.com/">Susan Jean Robertson</a>. She’s a web developer but her blog is mostly posts about her knitting projects and reaction posts to interesting long reads she finds. It’s so far away from the stuff I write about that I’m kind of jealous of her. I think she’d make a great interview candidate.</p>
<p><a href="https://brilliantcrank.com/">Greg Storey</a> is another recommendation I’d make, he’s a prolific blogger from the old days, but I feel he’s recently re-found his voice and is harnessing a deep punk rock aesthetic. Worth a read as well.</p>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>If you’re interested in stuff I do…. I blog at daverupert.com, I also post my <a href="https://daverupert.com/stories/">shitty sci-fi</a> on my site, I have a few apps like <a href="https://mundango.daverupert.com/">Mundango</a> hosted on subdomains. And I co-host <a href="https://shoptalkshow.com/">Shop Talk Show</a> with <a href="https://chriscoyier.net">Chris Coyier</a> from CodePen (<a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/pb-chris-coyier">and this blog</a>), it’s a weekly web development podcast. </p>
<p>Thank you so much for having me.</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>

    <title>James A. Reeves</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/james-a-reeves</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/6ZDDNzTLssJ860ZQ</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 13 Jun 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with James A. Reeves, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://www.jamesreeves.co">jamesreeves.co</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/james-a-reeves">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>Left-handed. Six feet tall. Becoming aggressively middle-aged and doing my best not to lapse into nostalgia even though being alive in the twenty-first century feels like an increasingly undignified experience.</p>
<p>Work-wise, I’m lucky. I’ve managed to stitch together a living that lets me do things I care about: designing things for constructive clients, teaching a class about the history of visual culture, and working with my partner Candy Chang on art installations about the future of ritual. I’m trying to do as much of this as I can before the robots and recessions get here.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>It started as Kinosport in 2000, back when I was heavy into <a href="https://www.moma.org/documents/moma_catalogue_250_300063174.pdf">film and Constructivism</a>. Then came a ten-year run as Big American Night during the Bush and Obama years when I crisscrossed the country listening to late-night AM radio, where America’s <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Paranoid_Style_in_American_Politics">paranoid style</a> was curdling into extreme tribalism. But looking in the rearview mirror now, it all seems rather quaint. </p>
<p>After some time overseas, I decided to nix the American focus, so I renamed it Atlas Minor, after one of the last maps to feature sea monsters. I thought this was a clever name until, several years later, someone took it for their design company. Rather than argue about it, I decided the name was a little pretentious anyway. </p>
<p>I’ve spent so much time chopping myself into pieces over the years: a blog for writing, a separate website for design work, another for music, and yet another for artwork. But last year, I woke up one morning with a rare revelation: I should just be James. So here we are.</p>
<p>I’m perpetually redesigning my website, hoping to achieve a Platonic blend of legibility and calm while also evoking the inside of my head, which is very much neither of those things. Fiddling with my website feels like rearranging the furniture: a cleansing, sometimes a humbling, when I’m forced to accept how I actually <em>live</em>. </p>
<p>One night I asked myself: what do I like to do when nobody’s paying attention? Well, I tend to make heavily reverberated mixtapes of slow-motion songs while ruminating about spiritual matters. So last year, I turned this tendency into a ritual: <a href="https://www.jamesreeves.co/radio/">Midnight Radio</a>—a short mix and an essay that I send out ‘round midnight on the first and fifteenth of every month.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>Ugly and splintered. For years I romanticized the <em>act</em> of writing to a destabilizing degree. I was convinced I should be producing lovely personal essays about <em>themes</em>, maybe even some punchy think-pieces about current events. But in reality, I had notebooks filled with tangled sentences about mythology, techno, death, petty grievances, highways, favorite songs, and neon lights.</p>
<p>I often think about <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2021/jun/19/douglas-coupland-on-generation-x-at-30-generational-trashing-is-eternal">Douglas Coupland’s confession</a> that “around 2010 my own brain started feeling truly different. I realised that I was never going to go back to my old, pre-internet brain: I’d been completely rewired.” This idea horrifies me on a spiritual level because sometimes it feels like an ultimatum: embrace a pixellated future without complaint or grieve for the textures of the past. </p>
<p>The only solution might be a cognitive leap, like how the Modernists plunged into the future a century ago, determined <a href="https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/485540">to fuse with the machine</a>. Embrace speed. Groove on distraction and fragments. Let my thoughts get garbled and strange. </p>
<p>But to be concrete about process: I always start with pen and paper. I think better when the writing doesn’t resemble the final product. For <a href="https://www.jamesreeves.co/destroyer-of-obstacles/">a recent piece</a>, I wrote a few sentences about a terrible visit to the dentist, which for some reason left me thinking about a fire ceremony I had the opportunity to see in Japan—how those taiko drums rattled my ribcage. I sensed a connection between these events, but I had to let it cook for a week before I saw the connective tissue: acceptance as liberation.</p>
<p>For this interview, I jotted “rearview mirrors” and “rearranging furniture” into my notebook and put it away for two weeks before typing it out in IA Writer, which is the only writing software I use these days.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>I used to believe my physical situation was very important. The perfect desk or café. A mystical belief that the right notebook would solve all my problems. I wasted <em>years</em> in absurd feedback loops in which, facing the blank page in the morning, I would decide I was a night owl who did his best writing at midnight, and when midnight rolled around, I would discover I was an early bird after all. And so on. </p>
<p>Maybe those calisthenics were necessary for me to finally—and truly—understand it’s very simple: Write or don’t write. So now I write whatever whenever. But I make sure to write every day or else I’ll need to go through a day or two of sighing and self-loathing before I get the muscles and momentum again.</p>
<h2>Can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>After twenty years on WordPress and a few on Substack, I switched to Ghost last year because it’s lighter and easier, and I wanted to start my Midnight Radio newsletter on a platform that feels secure and sane and not tinted by some tech guru’s tantrums. After so many years of thrashing around in the muck of bloated plugins and baroque template structures, working with a light combo of handlebars and static HTML is a pleasure.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>I would have started Midnight Radio sooner. But the teacher appears when the student is ready, etc. Putting together some text and sound before midnight on the 1st and 15th of every month has become a reassuring ritual that has helped me etch deeper memories and find unexpected connections between my favorite things. And it’s led to some delightful conversations with people I may not have otherwise met.</p>
<h2>How much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? What's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>The most important skill for surviving the 21st century is managing one’s attention, so the idea that someone is spending their time online with my writing feels like a gift, and I’m not about to charge money to receive that. </p>
<p>To my mind, “monetize your content” is one of the most bleak phrases in the English language. I wouldn’t want to meet the psychopath who would <em>pay</em> to receive more email. I prefer when people sell concrete things. This summer I’d like to make a little book that compiles the first year of Midnight Radio, and I might offer a few handsome prints of melancholy gas stations.</p>
<p>Anyway, between hosting and domain names, my current setup probably shakes out to $25 per month, but the spiritual cost is priceless.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p><a href="http://candychang.com">Candy Chang</a> because I want her to blog more often. David Leo Rice because <a href="https://southwestreview.com/volume-110-number-1/the-feast-of-fools-on-carnival-imagination-and-heresy-in-the-age-of-the-trickster/">this essay</a> captures our current gestalt like nothing else, and his <a href="https://wakeisland.substack.com">Wake Island dispatches</a> with Paul K have become required reading. And although <a href="http://martinessig.com">Marty Essig</a>’s website is often inscrutable, I know he’d be fascinating to interview, especially if you’re interested in talking about demons.</p>
<h2>Is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p><a href="https://www.patreon.com/collection/487611?view=expanded">Fall of Civilizations</a>, which might seem a bit on the nose nowadays, but I’ve learned so much: the wild technolgies of the Khmer Empire, how the Sumerians invented time, and the eerie Sea People who wiped out the Bronze Age. I fall asleep to an episode every night at 75% speed. It’s absolutely worth $3 a month to support Paul Cooper’s brilliant work—start with Carthage, but be warned: it’s a heartbreak.</p>
<p>And lately my late-night writing has been heavily soundtracked by Midwife’s <a href="https://heavenmetal.bandcamp.com/album/prayer-hands">heaven metal</a> and <a href="https://variantsonics.bandcamp.com/album/dreaming-thru-vector">hour-long reverb sessions</a> from the Deepchord camp.</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
        <p>Now that you're done reading the interview, <a href='https://www.jamesreeves.co'>go check the blog</a> and <a href='https://jamesreeves.co/rss'>subscribe to the RSS feed</a>.</p>
        <p>If you're looking for more content, go read one of the previous <a href='https://peopleandblogs.com' target='_blank'>139 interviews</a>.</p>

    <title>Benji</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/benji</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/JjttSR9RuCR7tG6q</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 06 Jun 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Benji, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://www.benji.dog">benji.dog</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/benji">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>Hi, I'm Benji and I'm a software engineer from Ecuador. I currently live in Minneapolis with my wife, our two kids, and our cat.</p>
<p>I moved to the US for university to study Computer Science. Originally, I was thinking of continuing on to do research as I had great experiences with the professors and projects I worked in but life happened and I found myself looking for jobs. A lot of what I had learned in university that far was less practical for the jobs I found myself applying to. Luckily, I ended up finding a job with amazing coworkers who I got to learn a ton from.</p>
<p>Professionally, I do a little bit of everything and jump between working on mobile and web apps. I like this level of change as it allows me to continue learning and working with different platforms and projects everyday.</p>
<p>When I'm not working, I'm usually building some new Lego or MagnaTiles structure with my kids, playing video games, or watching movies.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>Over the years I started several one-off blogs which usually followed the development of whatever project I was working on at the time. These were all short lived and never really got updated once I stopped working on the projects.</p>
<p>The biggest thing keeping me from starting a blog was that I couldn't settle on a name. I didn't want to use my full name and nothing else really worked for me. At some point in 2015 I found out that the Top Level Domain (TLD) <code>.dog</code> was a thing so I thought it would be funny to get the name "benji.dog" as most of the time when I introduce myself to someone and they learn my name they say: "oh, like the dog?". Maybe its just funny to me 😄.</p>
<p>Originally this was just a pretty basic landing page which linked out to other places. Some time later I started a "making websites" group at work as several coworkers were interested in having a their own personal websites. This is when I got interested in the <a href="https://indieweb.org">IndieWeb</a> and I started adding things as I found features in the wiki that I liked.</p>
<p>Today, my site is my primary place for publishing things I do. If I <a href="https://benji.dog/watched">watch</a> a movie, <a href="https://benji.dog/read">read</a> a book, <a href="https://benji.dog/bookmarks">bookmark</a> an interesting post, post a <a href="https://benji.dog/photos">photo</a>, or just generally want to write about <a href="https://benji.dog/feed/all">anything</a>, it goes on my site.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>Most of the posts on my site are either short notes or media tracking so I usually just write these on my phone and publish them immediately.</p>
<p>For the longer posts on my site, the process can vary wildly. I have written a whole post in an hour and published it right away and I have also published posts after having them in different stages of draft for years.</p>
<p>There are several posts in my drafts folder that I know I will never publish. I still find myself being highly critical of my writing and I find that writing a draft even if it will never be made public is good practice. I do revisit these drafts every so often in case any of the ideas there are good starting points for a new post.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>I've been working from home for a long time and my desk is really the only place where I can sit down and write or code anymore. This has more to do with comfort than creativity though.</p>
<p>I don't really think I have an ideal creative environment. I usually have a notebook and pen with me everywhere I go and I find myself writing down anything that comes to mind whether its writing out ideas or drawing little characters.</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>The current iteration of my site is built with <a href="https://www.11ty.dev">Eleventy</a> and I've been using that since 2019. All of the code for it is on <a href="https://github.com/benjifs/benji">GitHub</a> and whenever I make a change, the site gets rebuilt and deployed on <a href="https://netlify.com">Netlify</a>.</p>
<p>The bit that brings it all together is a separate project I wrote. It doesn't really have a name but since it's implementing a serverless <a href="https://indieweb.org/Micropub">micropub endpoint</a> I just named it <a href="https://github.com/benjifs/micropub">micropub</a> (I should change that). This is also deployed to Netlify and uses functions and GitHub's (or GitLab's) API to make commits and push new content to my site's repo. Since it's using micropub, I could then use any of the many different <a href="https://indieweb.org/Micropub/Clients">Micropub Clients</a> to add, edit, or remove new posts to my site.</p>
<p>A little over a year ago I decided to build my own micropub client so that I could add <a href="https://benji.dog/watched">movie watch posts</a> to my site directly instead of using a different platform for keeping track of that. This project is called <a href="https://sparkles.sploot.com/">sparkles</a> and if your site supports IndieAuth and Micropub, then you could also use this to write posts. It now supports most other type of posts so it's the only way I add things to my site now. Because I built it as a Progressive Web App (PWA), it's also on my phone's homescreen so I can easily create posts from anywhere.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>I have often thought that maybe my domain name wasn't the best choice as it's expensive and sometimes confusing to say out loud. I have yet to think of anything I like more and it still makes me smile.</p>
<p>Because I've been so comfortable with my current setup for so long, I haven't had a chance to try out all the different options out there. I do still very much like static site generators so I would probably like to try out other options now to see if I would still end up in the same place. But realistically, Eleventy does everything that I need it to do so it would take some serious convincing to get me to change that.</p>
<p>However, since I have less free time now than I used to when starting out, I would probably start with a selfhosted blogging solution and for that I really like <a href="https://goblog.app/">GoBlog</a>.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>I pay about $60/year for the two domain names I use for my site, one being a short domain to make links easier to share. That's the only real cost for my site as I'm still on Netlify's free tier and haven't really had any issues there. My site doesn't generate any revenue and this is something that I'm ok with for me.</p>
<p>It's great that there are so many different ways for people to make money from their blogs and if you want to do it, you should.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>I have a <a href="https://benji.dog/blogroll">blogroll</a> and I think all of those sites are amazing! I try to keep it updated as I discover new personal sites too.</p>
<p>As for who to interview next, I'd love to hear from:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://dead.garden">Jo</a></li>
<li><a href="https://artlung.com">Joe Crawford</a></li>
<li><a href="https://heyloura.com">Loura</a></li>
<li><a href="https://marisabel.nl">Marisabel</a></li>
<li><a href="https://nicksimson.com">Nick Simson</a></li>
<li><a href="https://thewallflowerdigest.co.uk">Alice @ The Wallflower Digest</a></li>
</ul>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p><a href="https://projects.kwon.nyc/internet-is-fun/">The internet used to be fun</a> is a collection of articles about the internet from the past and  I find the articles in this list inspiring. They also serve as a reminder to continue building the web that I want to see.</p>
<p>There are several online <a href="https://events.indieweb.org">IndieWeb Events</a> which are a great way to chat with others who share a love for personal websites. Even if you haven't yet started your site, the community here has been really inspiring to me.</p>
<p>Lastly, here is <a href="https://xoxofest.com/2024/videos/cabel-sasser/">Cabel Sasser's talk from XOXO 2024</a>. Ever since I first watched this, I've been reminding myself to "send the nice email" when I see someone's website I like. There's so many amazing things that people are creating on their websites and I think it's a good thing when we take a moment to tell each other that.</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>

    <title>Sebasti&#225;n Mon&#237;a</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/sebastian-monia</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/86HfstuQcnx7q25Z</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 30 May 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Sebastián Monía, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://site.sebasmonia.com">site.sebasmonia.com</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/sebastian-monia">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>My name is Sebastián, I was born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in the early 80s.</p>
<p>I have been working as a software developer since 2004. Over time I did a bit of everything in terms of technologies, but also roles: pure coding, team lead, analyst... I got into programming as a way to run more games in an aging 486 computer. I was 14, and I quickly realized that programming was not gonna free up more memory (unlike playing with config.sys and unloading stuff), but I got hooked into building little programs.</p>
<p>I was never good at building things with my hands, the abstractness of code suited me better :) It wasn't my first career choice. As a teen, I wanted to study astrophysics - inspired by a lot of Carl Sagan books. But I thought that if I did that, I would have to move to another country, and I didn't want to leave even my hometown. That's not the end of the ironies, I also thought that the alternative was to stay and end up in a teaching job, which I didn't think I was cut out for. Yet I became a TA in college (briefly) and after that experience, prepared talks and presentations at most of my jobs &gt;_&gt;</p>
<p>I live with my wife and son in New York City (if you are familiar with the NYC metro area: I don't really live in NYC). I spent 10 years in Denver before that (if you are familiar with the Denver metro area: I didn't really live in Denver). We moved to USA when our son was 8 months old, which was a bit stressing, but here we are. I was also still working on my engineering degree, which at this point I don't think I will ever complete.</p>
<p>Despite being Argentinian, I never cared for football, until the kiddo and I started attending Colorado Rapids games in Denver (at his request). Seeing the game live made me appreciate it and understand it in a new way. We are still fans, and we go to matches when they play close to NYC. Watching the games on TV is a weekly appointment for us. Football is one of our biggest topics, we talk players, tactics, tournaments. <em>I read football books</em>...combining passion with nerdom is fitting for me, I guess.</p>
<p>As for other hobbies and things I enjoy...</p>
<p>I love everything animated, from deeper adult-oriented movies to silly cartoons for kids. My favorite medium is stop motion, because it creates fantasy out of physical, tangible, things.</p>
<p>I have been getting back into reading, I used to complete a few books a year and for no particular reason I stopped at some point. A shame!</p>
<p>I also like playing videogames, rarely if ever online, and mostly independent (smaller) games.</p>
<p>I used to stargaze, but gave away my telescope right before moving here - I had stopped using it much.</p>
<p>I sometimes write code as a hobby, too.</p>
<p>I've been meaning to write an about page for my blog, I should totally copy and paste this :) Speaking of which...</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>I toyed with the idea of blogging many times over the years, when I was younger I used to write a lot. But as with many other things in life, I felt (blogging, writing open source, etc) was best left to people more qualified than me. I finally created a (very short lived) blog about configuring <a href="https://sebasmonia.github.io/">Emacs (a text editor) in Windows</a> in 2017. But publishing a new article was convoluted, and I didn't quite find the tone for it, so I abandoned it.</p>
<p>Speaking of Emacs, it is a 70s/80s editor, but has support for advanced features (like, undoing in only a portion of your document at a time, and multiple clipboards), which gave a new bar to evaluate technology. More importantly, it is also free and open software. And over time, the ideals of making technology accessible, open, free and privacy respecting, started getting into me.</p>
<p>In 2023, I found out about Gemini. Not the Google product! <a href="https://geminiprotocol.net/">A "protocol"</a>: a way to access pages that is not the Web, but its own thing. And it is really small, has no tracking etc. I found an easy to use service to publish a "capsule" (the Gemini term for page). So I created one! Which I won't link, because you need a special browser to access it.</p>
<p>That last point is what pushed me towards creating a regular Web blog. The true resistance to the modern, privacy invasive, and bloated web, isn't to go away to a different place. The best way to fight is from the inside: to stay in the web and keep it real, independent, interesting. Outside of walled gardens and social networks (yes, even Bluesky and Mastodon, the new darlings. Such a contrarian, I know).</p>
<p>My email service includes hosting of static files as web pages, I figured I could use that for the blog, and thus "Hoagie's small corner of the internet" was born :)</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>I have ideas at random times. Sometimes I write while waiting for something else to happen at work, other times I have ideas while walking, and make a quick note on my phone to write about them later. For a couple posts, the ideas come and go, simmering for a few days, until the way to go about them clicks. One time, I wrote about having no idea what to write about :)</p>
<p>I publish the text within a couple hours of typing it - and many times almost immediately, after a quick spell check. And then I have to go back and correct the text, because spelling is not the only thing that can go wrong when writing. Who knew... &gt;_&gt; </p>
<p>I only draft and revisit the (few) pure technical posts, to make sure that the code has no errors, and the explanations flow correctly.</p>
<p>So far, I haven't had to delete any content for being too silly/confidently wrong/hurtful, and maybe if that happened I would think of having someone proof reading the text. But on the other hand, I like the idea that my blog is stream-of-conscious-y.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>The one thing I would say I "need" to write is either my mechanical keyboard, or using my personal laptop (that happens to have a keyboard I like. Or that I am used to. Maybe both). It's the digital version of having the right pen.</p>
<p>Other than that, I can write anywhere. I noticed that the more personal a post is, the more likely it is that I write it at my desk, at night.</p>
<p>I do believe that the physical space can make a difference. I haven't tested it for a blog post yet, but I am one of <em>those people</em> who equate writing code with writing prose: closer to a craft than an engineering practice. I've been stuck in the past with a coding problem, and moving to a different area, or working from a coffee shop for a day, got the thoughts flowing again.</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>My hosting only supports static files, so that settled a lot of technical decisions right there. But I always knew I didn't want to tie myself to a tool (site generator, framework, etc). Part of the fun of the site was coming up with my own "publishing tools". So I write directly in HTML, and have a few commands in my editor to synchronize the content, add formatted footnotes, links to images, etc. The whole thing, can be found in <a href="https://git.sr.ht/~sebasmonia/site.sebasmonia.com">SourceHut</a>. I don't expect it to be re-usable at all, but you can take a look, if you are curious. The downside to this custom tooling, is that there are features that that are still unsupported, like tag navigation. Some day...</p>
<p>The domain is a subdomain of the one I used for my email, <code>sebasmonia.com</code>. Which is the why of the funky website URL, too.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>Well, speaking of the URL, it would be nice to have something...different. I am not sure what. The name is a mouthful, and while I don't care for concealing my identity in any way, having my full name <em>right there</em> feels...dorky :)</p>
<p>I know other sites do that too, but in my case it wasn't a conscious and confident choice. So, dorky.</p>
<p>Other than that, no, I wouldn't change too many things. The blogging is happening at a somewhat regular cadence (knocking wood), and the fact that I have a very simple site helps me publish often: I feel like I found my way of making it all work.</p>
<p>Sometimes I wish I should have started earlier! But then, I wouldn't have the same confidence to "put myself out there". Wishing for changes is a slippery slope...it happened when and how it happened for a reason. (Probably a less meaningful reason that we give the universe credit for. Usually chance. And that is OK, too.)</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>The blog is, in a way, free? Because I am paying for the email and domain anyway. But since that's a lame answer, here are the costs:</p>
<ul>
<li>Fastmail is USD60 a year. That includes email, calendar, notes, and most important, a WebDAV storage where I can expose a directory as a website. Which is a feature I didn't care about when I signed up for the service 🙃</li>
<li>The domain is USD15 a year. It used to be USD10. I sort of want it to get expensive enough that I justify getting a new domain, with a cooler name. But then I would have the pressure of choosing a new name!</li>
</ul>
<p>My position regarding monetization: I think people should do whatever works for them.</p>
<p>One of the curious changes I had when I became more concerned about free software and privacy and all that jazz, is that I am more likely to pay for my tools and services. Example, paid email instead of Outlook.com/GMail/etc. And I started donating to people who wrote libraries and tools I found useful. I have made small donations, here and there, to independent websites, too.</p>
<p>In my own blog, I don't see the need. I think if I monetized it (which I hadn't considered until this question), I would write thinking of an audience, it would spoil the mmmmm voice? I have right now.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>This is a difficult one, as I am working through the list of People and Blogs to keep adding bookmarks :) But excluding people already featured in P&amp;B, a few recommendations:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.rousette.org.uk/">BSAG (But she's a girl)</a>, a fun blog. Random topics.</li>
<li><a href="https://82mhz.net/">Andreas 82Mhz</a>, another fun blog, and more random topics.</li>
<li><a href="https://berthub.eu/articles/">Bert Hubert</a>, writes about tech and sometimes science. With an eye towards their impact on society, and regulations around them.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.schneier.com/">Bruce Schneier</a>, a very well known author and speaker. He writes about cryptography and information security, but he too focuses more on the human and societal aspects rather the pure tech stuff (in his blog at least).</li>
</ul>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>To no one's surprise, if they ever read my site, or made it this far in the interview, I will share some random commentary :)</p>
<ul>
<li>I think <a href="https://marginalia-search.com/">marginalia-search.com</a> and <a href="https://wiby.me/">wiby.me</a> are really cool services. I also like that webrings made a come back, and at some point I'll surely join a couple.</li>
<li>Staying in the loop of the news is very different from buying into the media frenzy (on any side of the political spectrum). The world is better place than we are being told. And while a lot of things need to change, to make that happen we can't be frozen from sensory overload. Or rage. Or fear.</li>
<li>Semi-related: quit all social networks. Just do it. I know it is hard, but you can. How do I know it is hard? because I am trying to quit myself :D and trying and trying and...</li>
<li>In doesn't matter if a change you make is a drop in an ocean: as long as your drop matters to you, do it anyway. Whether is recycling, buying less things you don't need, voting, using your car less. Everything adds up.</li>
<li>Slow down. Add <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/indieweb-carnival-on-the-importance-of-friction">friction</a> to your life. Meditate, breathe, take a stroll. Have a cup of tea (or, sip from your <em>mate</em>, if you are a southern South American).</li>
</ul>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
        <p>Now that you're done reading the interview, <a href='https://site.sebasmonia.com'>go check the blog</a> and <a href='https://site.sebasmonia.com/feed.xml'>subscribe to the RSS feed</a>.</p>

    <title>Seth Werkheiser</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/seth-werkheiser</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/IEbwGC3M6qrCRoEi</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 23 May 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Seth Werkheiser, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://sethw.xyz">sethw.xyz</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/seth-werkheiser">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>It's all my parents doing, really. They had a Texas Instruments TI-99/4a in the house, and would get computer game magazines and type out the games when I went to bed, so I woke up and had a new game to play in the morning. This got me a bit interested in programming, at least. Or that, just to know I could do something on the computer, and make a thing. And that really changed my world when I bought my first computer... it was a Pacakard Bell I got from Sears with a charge card. It was like $3000 with the monitor, and had a Pentium 100 chip or something like that. Anyways - it was with that machine I started dabbling with "desktop publishing," but then making websites. That was 1995 or so, I think. I learned I could view the source code of something like <a href="http://cnn.com/">CNN.com</a>, save it locally and load it up again with the new goofy headlines I made.</p>
<p>But my background is two-fold. I'm a third generation musician, too. Music is my first love. Or rather, I love music and computers pretty much the same. Once I figured out I wasn't going to be a rock star, I started a music blog in 2001 called Buzzgrinder, and that literally changed my life, and is the foundation of where I am today.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>I wish I had kept a blog going back to those early 2000 years, but really I got back into blogging in 2018. I've found some bits and pieces of blogs and articles I wrote via the Wayback machine, and just copy and pasted them back onto my blog. I've also taken photos I uploaded to Flickr dating back to 2004, and put them along with the captions I wrote on the site, too. So right now the blog spans from 2004 to 2025, over 21 years of writing and photos, which blows my mind.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>Oh, it's all off the cuff. Shooting from the hip. I might go a few days without writing here and there, but that's mostly because I write a newsletter called Social Media Escape Club, so that's two bigger pieces a week.</p>
<p>But I never really draft anything. I might make a few edits during the writing process, but anything on the site is mostly from me opening a new browser tab, banging something out, and hitting publish. Zero planning, all vibes.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>The ideal creative environment is being as far away from the computer as possible. I'm an avid trail runner, so most weekdays and every weekend I'm in the woods, climbing hills, and getting into some creeks. It's not like I get a bunch of "content ideas" when I'm out there, like the whole "I get all my best ideas in the shower" thing. I think it's more the focus required, and the tangible danger of snakes or twisting an ankle, and the immense beauty of nature that clears my head and allows some of the magic to sneak into my brain on occasion when I do sit down at the computer and get ready to write.</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>I sometimes capture ideas in the Bear app. I go on a lot of walks throughout the day - again, I just need to get away from the computer a lot - so I'll sometimes type something there, or dictate it. I also use Voice Notes, too, when I'm driving. Not that I usually go back and take the transcription literally and paste it somewhere, and work on it. But I think the physical speaking of the idea is what helps it marinate and stick around.</p>
<p>Domain names are stored at Hover. The blog is built on WordPress. My friend Tom runs <a href="https://iheartblank.net/">I Heart Blank</a>. He does WordPress development and hosting, so he handles all of that for me. We met years decades ago during the time when I played music regularly, and have stayed friends, and now I pay him every year to host the blog.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>Honestly, no. WordPress and the hosting and such works fine for me. I don't care much about the name, or the theme, or whatever. The blog is 100% for me.</p>
<p>"I write to remember," as the lyrics go in 'One Armed Scissor' by At the Drive In.</p>
<p>I write the stuff I write about just so in two years, or 10, I can go back and see where I was at, that's it. I write about races I ran, or go back sometimes to the COVID days, or to see the little projects I started then stopped doing three months later.</p>
<p>I think the most important thing about writing a blog is the actual writing. There's 1000 different blog platforms, 1000 different themes, unlimited domain name ideas... none of it matters to me, really. I'd rather just have a place where I can write publicly, and people can read it if they want.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>I think hosting is like $120 a year? It's not a whole lot. Tom takes good care of me, and I tell all my friends who are thinking about a WordPress site to go to him, so it's a mutually beneficial friendship like that! The site doesn't make any money. I've got a Ko-fi link, but no one clicks it. It's fine. Like I said, the blog is mostly for me! I mean, I know some people read it, but I don't check the stats or the referrals. I don't care. I don't have comments. I get an email once every few months from someone who read something, which is great.</p>
<p>But hey - if people want to monetize their own blog? Do it! These are wild times we're living in right now. If you can pay the phone bill or rent by updating a blog a few times a week, then I support that 100%.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>Multiple times a day I hit up <a href="https://daringfireball.net">Daring Fireball</a>. I'm less of a Mac enthusiast these days, but John Gruber has things to say about a lot of things, so I'm always checking it out.</p>
<p>I'm always stoked to see <a href="https://www.ericafustero.com">Erica Fustero's</a> colorful and whimsical updates.</p>
<p>There'a always delight and cool things to check out on <a href="https://www.swiss-miss.com">Swiss Miss</a>.</p>
<p><a href="https://seths.blog/">Seth Godin</a> recently posted his 10,000 post. Hope to stick around long enough to read the next 10,000.</p>
<p>Oh, and you should interview <a href="https://jasper.tandy.is/">Jasper Tandy</a> next. He's always linking to interesting things and taking gorgeous photographs.</p>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>I've been writing the <a href="https://socialmediaescapeclub.substack.com">Social Media Escape Club</a> newsletter since October of 2021, and having lots of fun with that. It started as a battle cry to delete the apps and put down our phones, but it's turned into a wonderful community of creative people helping one another navigate the world without algorithms and relying less on big platforms. It's been a lot of fun, and through this project I've got to meet so many wonderful people. It reminds me a lot of the early blogging days!</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
        <p>Now that you're done reading the interview, <a href='https://sethw.xyz'>go check the blog</a> and <a href='https://sethw.xyz/feed/'>subscribe to the RSS feed</a>.</p>

    <title>Watts Martin</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/watts-martin</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/ZaCh3XG308CmPa71</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 16 May 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Watts Martin, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://coyotetracks.org/blog/">coyotetracks.org/blog</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/watts-martin">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>I’ve been a technical writer for a little over a decade now, after a previous decade and change as a web developer. I’ve been a writer of one sort or another for as long as I can remember—when I’m not writing for the job, I’m often off at a coffee shop or craft brewery working on a science fiction or fantasy story. (Or occasionally a blog post.)</p>
<p>Other than too much writing, I like traveling—both around the United States and just on day trips around my local area. Right now, that local area is the middle of nowhere, Florida, about fifty miles north of Tampa and fifty miles west of Orlando; on Saturdays I’m usually puttering somewhere around one of those two metro areas. I also love tiki bars in the mold of Trader Vic’s and Don the Beachcomber’s; while you might imagine Florida is full of tiki bars, it’s actually full of <em>beach</em> bars, not at all the same thing.</p>
<p>For roughly the first two decades of this century, I lived around the San Francisco Bay Area, which is much more my vibe as far as climate, geography, culture, and politics—basically everything except housing costs. I’m in Florida for family reasons, so I don’t regret moving back, but sometimes I wish I’d found a way to swing moving my mother to the West Coast rather than moving myself here.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>Huh. Well, I’ve had something <em>resembling</em> a blog for an absurdly long time, going back to the LiveJournal days. Coyote Tracks got started on Tumblr when I decided to sort of “soft reboot” it—I’d been trying to tumble-blog and failing—and began writing musings on tech, particularly Apple. Like many people around that time, I was inspired by John Gruber of Daring Fireball.</p>
<p>I tried several other platforms after Tumblr, although to this day I’d argue it’s severely underrated given what you get for essentially nothing. WordPress was in there at one point, and I think I tried something else I’ve forgotten before moving to Micro.blog for a few years. Most recently I’ve gone back to self-hosting.</p>
<p>As for the name “Coyote Tracks,” I don’t know if I have a <em>great</em> reason. I’m a semi-closeted furry who likes coyotes, and as mentioned, I’m pretty peripatetic.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>I keep a list of ideas for articles, but also sometimes just get inspired by stories I happen to come across—a news article, another blog post, a social media post, whatever. Sometimes posts will come together in an afternoon, other times they’ll kick around for days, depending on how much research they need. The <em>very</em> long post in which I used an “AI novel writer” to see if it was as bad as I expected (spoiler: yes) took quite a while.</p>
<p>Lately, I’ve been writing (and keeping the list of ideas) in <a href="https://obsidian.md">Obsidian</a>. I’ve used other tools over the years: <a href="https://ulysses.app">Ulysses</a> (which is what I write most of my fiction in, after moving there from <a href="https://www.literatureandlatte.com/scrivener/overview">Scrivener</a>), <a href="https://ia.net/writer">iA Writer</a>, and <a href="https://www.barebones.com/products/bbedit/">BBEdit</a> (still my favorite tool for technical writing). In Obsidian, I use a <a href="https://languagetool.org/">LanguageTool</a> plug-in for a semi-automatic proofing pass; this is the same technology Ulysses uses for its “revision mode.” (I don’t use LanguageTool’s new “AI” features, for the record.) For both of those, I also use <a href="https://marked2app.com">Marked</a> as a preview tool, turning on its keyword highlighter to show oft-overused words, passive verbs, that sort of thing. I do this all for fiction, too, by the way. LanguageTool almost always catches something I missed, even if it frets that I use the word “fuck” too much.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>I think the space <em>does</em> influence my creativity, but I don’t know if I have an ideal environment—it depends on my mood. At home, I have an office space set up with lots of natural light, a nice keyboard, and an overpriced office chair. Sometimes I get my best writing done when I’m out, though. If I really want to go out and sit somewhere to <em>work,</em> I’ll take my iPad and a low-profile <a href="https://www.keychron.com/collections/low-profile-keyboard-collection/products/keychron-k3-wireless-mechanical-keyboard">Keychron K3 mechanical keyboard</a> that fits in the same bag, and sit down at a coffee shop or, better yet, a brewery. (Macs are better for editing/publishing, but iPads are as good, if not better, for doing first drafts.)</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>My website, including the blog, is generated with <a href="https://www.getzola.org">Zola</a>, a static site generator similar to Hugo. I maintain it, and publish it, with Panic’s <a href="https://nova.app">Nova</a>—I have tasks configured so I can press a button to run a local preview, and press another button to deploy it.</p>
<p>My blog also supports webmentions now—when I make a post, the link goes out on Bluesky and Mastodon, and if someone favorites that link, reposts it, or replies to it, that gets sent back to the blog and shows up under the post. This is handled using a Rube Goldberg machine comprised of <a href="https://brid.gy">Bridgy</a>, <a href="https://webmention.io">Webmention.io</a>, and <a href="https://github.com/chipotle/get-mentions">get-mentions</a>, a small client-side bit of JavaScript I wrote.</p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>I don’t know; I like static site generators, and appreciate that most of what I’ve done is pretty “close to the metal”. Having said that, Zola is better at building websites than it is at building blogs—it has absolutely zero special handling for blog articles, and the more posts you write, the more unwieldy it gets.</p>
<p>I suspect if I moved to another system, it would end up being <a href="https://ghost.org">Ghost</a>, or maybe a CMS like <a href="https://craftcms.com">Craft</a>. I’d probably avoid WordPress; as nice as it would be to have such a huge ecosystem, their new block-based editor seems actively hostile to people who just want to, you know, <em>write.</em> And Matt Mullenweg needs to do for WordPress what Markus Persson did for Minecraft, by which I mean disappear and never be heard from again.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetizing personal blogs?</h2>
<p>I’m hosting the blog on <a href="https://www.hetzner.com">Hetzner</a>, so it’s €4.49/month, which is just over $5/month at current exchange rates. So, it’s as close to free as you can realistically get. While I have a <a href="https://ko-fi.com/wattsmartin">Ko-Fi</a> set up, people mostly don’t bite.</p>
<p>If you figure out how to monetize a personal blog, I mean, more power to you, right? There's an alternate universe where I <em>did</em> figure that out sometime around 2012—I got linked to semi-regularly by bigger blogs, sometimes by Techmeme, was a featured technology blog on Tumblr, all that. I was never a “big name,” but I probably made it to medium name.</p>
<p>Even so, putting Google Ads on my Tumblr—remember when that was a thing?—earned me like seven bucks. Before I tried anything else, I ended up getting my first tech writing job at a startup whose founders had been reading my blog. So, I suppose you could say I <em>did</em> find a way to monetize…just not directly.</p>
<p>I think newsletters are interesting as a strategy, and I might try to start one—but I feel like I’d have to be a more consistent blogger to pull that off.</p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>I’m going to be a dingus here and recommend two blogs that are technically newsletters. Since they’re both on Buttondown, though, you can read them on the web and subscribe to their RSS feeds, so they’re kind of blog-shaped.</p>
<p>First, <a href="https://buttondown.com/monteiro/archive/">Mike Monteiro’s Good News</a> is amazing—every article takes the premise of answering a “how to” question, from “how to make a book” to “how to choose a donut,” and turns it into a beautiful rhapsody of righteous leftist politics and warm-hearted compassion, and he’s a ferociously good writer.</p>
<p>Next, science fiction and fantasy author Charlie Jane Anders has a newsletter/blog called <a href="https://buttondown.com/charliejane/archive/">Happy Dancing</a> that talks about writing, politics, and sci-fi/pop culture news, all in her beautifully quirky style.</p>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>Let’s see. The aforementioned Charlie Jane Anders co-hosts a podcast with her former co-worker from io9 (and also a great writer), Annalee Newitz, called <a href="https://www.ouropinionsarecorrect.com">Our Opinions Are Correct</a>, which explores the connections between science fiction and real life. It’s often a lot of fun, and the episodes are kept to a reasonable length.</p>
<p>And, even if you’re <em>not</em> particularly into science fiction and fantasy but you’re into incredibly well-crafted short stories, I’d recommend a collection from last decade called <a href="https://smallbeerpress.com/books/2012/09/11/at-the-mouth-of-the-river-of-bees/"><em>At the Mouth of the River of Bees</em> by Kij Johnson</a>. All  the pieces in it are weird and literate and beautiful. And if you’re an aspiring genre writer, look into her novel-writing course—or Chris McKitterick’s short story course—at <a href="https://adastra-sf.com">the Ad Astra Institute</a>, a residential workshop in Lawrence, Kansas that used to be part of KU until the college decided to institute a policy against being interesting. My own novel, <a href="https://coyotetracks.org/for-sale/#kismet"><em>Kismet</em></a>, probably wouldn’t have ever been finished, let alone be as good, without that workshop, and I’ve returned to Lawrence a few times as a “graduate.”</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
        <p>Now that you're done reading the interview, <a href='https://coyotetracks.org/blog/'>go check the blog</a> and <a href='https://coyotetracks.org/blog/atom.xml'>subscribe to the RSS feed</a>.</p>

</item>                                <item>
    <title>Anh</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/anh</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/eTsbac0PIcZ0XiH5</guid>
    <pubDate>Fri, 09 May 2025 13:00:00 +0200</pubDate>
    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Anh, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://anhvn.com">anhvn.com</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/anh">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>I'm Anh, a designer and artist based in Canada. My hobbies include, predictably: making and looking at websites, drawing, playing video games, and collecting all of the above on my website.</p>
<p>By day—and also by night, because I maintain chaotic working hours—I design web things at a nice company.</p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>I've been Online™ for a long time, and I suppose I've always been "blogging" in some way for years—I'm much more comfortable with writing than speaking, and I'm a weird shy nerd, so I've always drifted towards oversharing on the internet. </p>
<p>anhvn.com started back in 2020 when I decided I would stop using a pseudonym and actually post stuff under my name that people would see. Before that, I had a blog that maybe three friends of mine knew about and looked at, which was freeing but also very lonely. I used to share more personal things then too, like what I did day-to-day or things I was struggling with, but now I'm more private about that. I appreciate vulnerability, but I'm more wary these days for privacy's sake.</p>
<p>anhvn.com is also more than just a blog—as a personal website, it's where I put other interests: unfinished notes and references ("the digital garden"); artwork I post on social media ("the sketchbook"); tracking the media I consume, like movies and books ("the media diary"). I like the freedom of being able to put whatever I want on it and designing how it's showcased.</p>
<p>“anhvn” stands for, of course, <a href="https://anhvn.com/vn">“anh visual novel.”</a> (JK, this is just one of my former homepages.) I've used a lot of different names online over the years, and I've also grown out of a lot of them. I based this domain on my actual name because I know I won't be tired of it in a decade or two.</p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>I write "weeknotes" consistently, though not at an actual weekly cadence. To write them, I'm usually pulling from some archive rather than trying to remember what I did—I'll look at my watchlist to see what I last watched; I'll go through my bookmarks app to see what cool links I've saved; I'll scroll through my own social media to see what I've posted about. This all gets dumped into a Markdown document in VS Code, and I keep adding to it and writing until I think I've covered everything or I grow sick of it.</p>
<p>When I'm tired of my usual blogging ways, I'll switch up the format. I've recently started doing <a href="https://anhvn.com/posts/2025/weeknotes-28/">chat-style posts</a>—i.e. posts that are formatted like text messages—which are more casual and freeing to write. Once in a while, I'll design <a href="https://anhvn.com/posts/2025/weeknotes-30/">a new blog post layout</a> just for a single post, because I'm bored of my current site design and want to play with some different fonts or colours. Sometimes this starts in Figma, and sometimes I do it directly in the browser.</p>
<p>I never have anyone review my posts before I publish, but I'd probably introduce that step in the future if I ever write anything more ambitious—all of my blog posts are quite informal. I do the most minimal of proofreading myself.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>It depends on the creative activity. For computer stuff, I work best when I'm at home—I need the ergonomics of a full desk setup, otherwise I feel slowed down. When writing, I need to be alone (also, preferably, on my regular computer setup), otherwise I can't focus. In my ideal world, I'm designing and writing in the morning while drinking my first coffee of the day.</p>
<p>I like drawing just about anywhere though. Unlike designing or writing, which involve a lot of paring down nebulous ideas into something presentable, drawing feels more expansive and benefits from external stimuli.</p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>My site is built with <a href="https://www.11ty.dev/">Eleventy</a>, a static site generator. It's perfect for me: relatively straight-forward to set up, flexible in how to structure my content, and has a large community. I have a lot of custom pages on my site because it's so easy to set up a new one. And of course, I've written <a href="https://anhvn.com/posts/2024/my-eleventy-site-setup/">a post about this</a>.</p>
<p>I host all my code on GitHub, and deploy it through Netlify. My domain is registered on Namecheap. It works fine! I don't really know how it all works under the hood—I don't know what npm is, and it's fine—but setting it up was straight-forward enough, and it hasn't broken on me yet, which is a great relief.  </p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>I would perhaps take tagging/categorizing more seriously—my blog archive has now grown to a point where it's unwieldy to peruse, and I'll need to go back and tag things for when I add post filtering. Otherwise, I'm quite satisfied with where it's at.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>My domain costs $15.88/year (a steal, really, for a five-letter .com domain of my own incredibly common name). That's the only website cost; I don't pay anything for GitHub or Netlify, and my company pays for my Adobe account, which allows me to use their webfonts.</p>
<p>My website generates zero revenue, which I'm perfectly fine with. If I find myself in a situation where I need to generate income though, I'm sure that would change. I've entertained thoughts of monetising in some way for years—such as through selling digital goods, taking art commissions, or having a ko-fi donations account—but I don't need to right now and that's not a burden I want to take on without good reason. I enjoy having the freedom to do whatever I want online; if I turn it into a business, then that comes with its own set of responsibilities and expectations.</p>
<p>That door isn't closed, though. At the end of the day, we all need to pay rent, so I'm all for blog monetisation. </p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.wavebeem.com/blog/">wavebeem's blog</a>  — Sage writes about their various side projects, blog redesigns (frequent! love it), and interests.</li>
<li><a href="https://blueludebar.com/journal">A.C. Esguerra</a> writes about journaling and art — exactly the kind of art blogging I want to read more of! </li>
<li><a href="https://making.melanie-richards.com/">Melanie Richards' fiber crafts blog</a> is the kind of hobby blogging I want to <em>do</em> more of.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.ninnsalaun.com/today">Reports from Unknown Places</a> by Ninn Salaün—does this count as a blog? you can follow it on RSS!—is a wonderful art project with daily posts about the weather.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>Floating around in the back of my mind, always, are comics—two very cool things you should check out are the <a href="https://comicsdevices.com/">Comics Devices Library</a> and <a href="https://digitalcomics.co/">Standards, Semantics, &amp; Sequential Art</a>. And then I humbly offer you my budding <a href="https://anhvn.com/garden/webcomics/">thoughts on webcomics</a>, from my digital garden.</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
        <p>Now that you're done reading the interview, <a href='https://anhvn.com'>go check the blog</a> and <a href='https://anhvn.com/feed.xml'>subscribe to the RSS feed</a>.</p>

    <title>Alexandra Deschamps-Sonsino</title>
    <link>https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/alexandra-deschamps-sonsino</link>
    <guid isPermaLink="true">https://manuelmoreale.com/@/page/O42dTTkDf1Pm07Lm</guid>

    <description><![CDATA[
        <p>This week on the People and Blogs series we have an interview with Alexandra Deschamps-Sonsino, whose blog can be found at <a href="https://www.designswarm.com">designswarm.com</a>.</p>
        <p>Tired of RSS? <a href="https://manuelmoreale.com/interview/alexandra-deschamps-sonsino">Read this in your browser</a> or <a href="https://buttondown.com/peopleandblogs">sign up for the newsletter</a>.</p>
        <p>People and Blogs is supported by the <em>"One a Month"</em> club members.</p>
        <p>If you enjoy P&B, <a href="https://ko-fi.com/manuelmoreale">consider becoming one</a> for as little as 1 dollar a month.</p>
        <hr>
        <h2>Let's start from the basics: can you introduce yourself?</h2>
<p>My name is <a href="https://www.designswarm.com/about/">Alexandra Deschamps-Sonsino</a> and I’m an author and consultant with a background in product and interaction design. I studied at <a href="https://interactiondesigninstituteivrea.org/">IDII</a> which was one of the pioneering post-graduate courses in interaction design and I’ve lived in London for 18 years. I was the first UK distributor of the Arduino and three of my projects are in the permanent collection of art of design museums around the world but these days I tend to work as a <a href="https://www.designswarm.com/work/">leader in organisations with a climate mission</a>. When I’m not working, I’m trying to get my feet all the way to the ground in downward dog and teaching myself how to knit. </p>
<h2>What's the story behind your blog?</h2>
<p>When I was studying at IDII in 2005 and I had a class with <a href="https://www.yanivsteiner.com/">Yaniv Steiner</a> who forced us to start our own <a href="http://wordpress.org/">Wordpress.org</a> instance to document our masters project. I hated figuring out PHP but eventually got the hang of it and just kindof kept going with it. My friends started doing <a href="https://interconnected.org/home/2018/07/24/weeknotes">weeknotes</a> but I always had a problem with the intimacy of the format. I was never a Livejournal kind of girl and don’t really like writing about my personal life outside of the <a href="https://www.designswarm.com/blog/2024/12/end-of-year-review-6/">end of year reviews</a> <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Wright_Steenson">Molly Steenson</a> started me on. So I keep things pretty professional or abstract. It helps that I live in England where people love cryptic crossword puzzles. </p>
<h2>What does your creative process look like when it comes to blogging?</h2>
<p>These days, I have two types of blog posts. A link dump I call <a href="https://www.designswarm.com/blog/category/sundayscraps/">’Sunday Scraps’</a> which lets me close some tabs on my phone and regular work-related musings. I never have a plan, I just try to blog regularly. I find it a useful way to practice writing in addition to writing books. If I go back to my earlier blog posts, I can see a tangible improvement in my English (my mother tongue is French) so that’s pleasing. I usually write later in the day, probably after I’ve been mulling over a blog post idea for a few days. I write in about an hour or less and I rarely write drafts. If I can’t seem to finish a blog post, I take that as a sign that it’s not going to be very good so I just close my laptop. Sometimes I go back to it, sometimes I don’t and just start a brand new one. I’m very aware people don’t read so I try to make my point inside of 600 words. I also never post my blog post content on other platforms. I know it’s a little bit pointless now with LLMs but my writing is my copyright, not anyone else’s.</p>
<h2>Do you have an ideal creative environment? Also do you believe the physical space influences your creativity?</h2>
<p>I have written too many blog posts on my very uncomfortable sofa to think that physical space has anything to do with my blogging. And I’m a big fan of <a href="https://allpoetry.com/poem/14326888-air-and-light-and-time-and-space-by-Charles-Bukowski">Bukowski’s 1992 poem ‘air and light and time and space’</a> which <a href="https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/04/charles-bukowski-air-and-light-and-time-and-space/">puts that idea to bed</a>. If you have something to say, you always find a way. </p>
<h2>A question for the techie readers: can you run us through your tech stack?</h2>
<p>I host the subdomain <a href="http://designswarm.com/blog">designswarm.com/blog</a> with dreamhost and the blog is a <a href="http://wordpress.com/">Wordpress.com</a> instance that is linked to it. </p>
<h2>Given your experience, if you were to start a blog today, would you do anything differently?</h2>
<p>Not really, I mean you’re just adding words to the internet. Unless you need to make a living from it, just write like nobody’s reading. Unless you’re being a wanker, in which case, don’t. Just go to the pub with your mates.</p>
<h2>Financial question since the Web is obsessed with money: how much does it cost to run your blog? Is it just a cost, or does it generate some revenue? And what's your position on people monetising personal blogs?</h2>
<p>I don’t take donations, I don’t have a substack, I don’t use Medium anymore (I extracted my posts from there years ago) and I generally don’t trust third party platforms for bloggers. I also don’t think I should be paid for my blog posts because they’re a calling card. The good stuff comes from people who read me and then want to work with me. If I was to charge for it, I’d limit the number of people who might want to work with me which is silly. And I have <a href="https://www.designswarm.com/books/">books</a> people can buy or borrow from their local library instead. So that’s enough monetisation of thoughts for one person I think. </p>
<h2>Time for some recommendations: any blog you think is worth checking out? And also, who do you think I should be interviewing next?</h2>
<p>I’m a big fan of <a href="https://www.thingsmagazine.net/">things magazine</a> which has been going for a long time. My friend <a href="https://buttondown.com/russell">Russell</a> also blogs about <a href="https://buttondown.com/russell/archive/">5 things</a> he finds interesting and there’s always some lovely things in there. You should talk to him and <a href="https://interconnected.org/home/">Matt Webb</a> about blogging. </p>
<h2>Final question: is there anything you want to share with us?</h2>
<p>If Scottee wrote a blog, I would read it. In the meantime, I really enjoy his annual <a href="https://scottee.co.uk/shinfo">podcast</a>.</p>        <hr>
        <h3>Keep exploring</h3>
